papers.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of cellular heterogeneity in Alzheimer disease.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how single-cell and spatial transcriptomic techniques have revealed the diversity of brain cell types and states involved in Alzheimer's disease. It discusses how different cell populations, including neurons, microglia, and astrocytes, show distinct gene expression changes depending on their location and disease stage. The work highlights how combining single-cell resolution with spatial context helps map disease progression across brain regions.
papers.why: Understanding spatial transcriptomic approaches to cellular heterogeneity in neurodegeneration directly informs methodology for mapping mitophagy and autophagy changes in neurons and interneurons within their spatial brain context.
papers.figure: A figure showing spatial mapping of cell-type-specific gene expression changes across brain regions affected by Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Live Spatial Transcriptomics Enables Longitudinal Tissue Mapping
papers.summary: This paper introduces a method called Live Spatial Transcriptomics, which allows researchers to measure gene expression patterns within tissue while keeping the tissue alive over time. Unlike traditional spatial transcriptomics that requires fixing and destroying samples, this approach enables repeated measurements from the same tissue sample at different timepoints. This longitudinal capability opens up new possibilities for tracking dynamic biological processes as they unfold spatially within living tissue.
papers.why: Live spatial transcriptomics could allow tracking of dynamic mitophagy and autophagy processes in neurons over time within the same tissue, potentially revealing how interneuron states and perineuronal net remodeling evolve rather than relying on static snapshots.
papers.figure: Figure demonstrating the longitudinal tissue mapping workflow showing repeated spatial transcriptomic measurements from the same living tissue sample at multiple timepoints.

papers.title: Brain clearance of protein aggregates in degenerative diseases: the role of microglia and astrocytes.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how microglia and astrocytes clear misfolded protein aggregates, such as amyloid-beta and tau, from the brain in neurodegenerative diseases. It likely discusses the cellular mechanisms these glial cells use, including phagocytosis and autophagy-related pathways, to degrade or transport aggregated proteins. It probably also addresses how dysfunction in these clearance systems contributes to disease progression.
papers.why: Although focused on glial cells rather than neurons, this work is relevant because glial clearance mechanisms share pathways with neuronal mitophagy/autophagy and may interact with interneuron health and perineuronal net integrity in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics maps region and isoform specific brain alterations in mdx and mdx<sup>4cv</sup> models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
papers.summary: This paper uses spatial transcriptomics to study brain tissue from mdx and mdx4cv mouse models of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which lack specific dystrophin isoforms. The analysis reveals that gene expression changes occur in a region-specific and isoform-specific manner across different brain areas. These findings help explain the varied cognitive and behavioral phenotypes seen in DMD models depending on which dystrophin isoforms are missing.
papers.why: The spatial transcriptomics methodology and region-specific brain mapping approach demonstrated here are directly relevant to applying spatial transcriptomics to study neuronal subpopulations and region-specific alterations in the context of interneurons and perineuronal nets.

papers.title: Mapping the Metabolic Landscape of Aging: Advances in Spatial Metabolomics for Deciphering Heterogeneity in Age-Related Diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews recent progress in spatial metabolomics, a technology that allows researchers to measure small molecules and metabolites directly within tissue sections while preserving their spatial location. It focuses on how this approach can reveal metabolic heterogeneity across different cell types and tissue regions during aging. The review highlights applications to age-related diseases, showing how spatial metabolic maps can uncover disease-specific metabolic signatures that bulk tissue analysis would miss.
papers.why: Since the PhD project integrates spatial metabolomics with spatial transcriptomics to study mitophagy and autophagy changes in aging neurons and interneurons, this review could inform methodological choices and highlight relevant age-related metabolic signatures applicable to perineuronal net and interneuron research.

papers.title: Involvement of PINK1-related mitophagy and necroptosis in TDI-induced experimental asthma.
papers.summary: This paper studies toluene diisocyanate (TDI)-induced asthma in an animal model, focusing on how mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to airway inflammation. It examines the role of PINK1-mediated mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared, and its connection to necroptosis, a form of programmed cell death. The findings suggest that disrupted mitophagy and necroptosis pathways may drive the pathology seen in occupational asthma triggered by chemical exposure.
papers.why: Although focused on lung tissue rather than brain, this paper is tangentially relevant for its mechanistic insights into PINK1-mediated mitophagy, a core pathway also central to neuronal mitophagy studies.

papers.title: FSP1 as the convergent hub of autophagy and ubiquitination governing ferroptosis in monocrotaline-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension.
papers.summary: This paper studies FSP1, a protein that protects cells from ferroptosis (an iron-dependent form of cell death), in a rat model of pulmonary arterial hypertension induced by monocrotaline. The researchers show that FSP1 acts as a central node linking autophagy and ubiquitination pathways to control whether cells undergo ferroptosis. Their findings suggest FSP1 could be a therapeutic target for this lung vascular disease.
papers.why: While focused on lung vasculature rather than brain, this work offers mechanistic insight into how autophagy and ubiquitination pathways converge to regulate cell death, a theme directly relevant to understanding mitophagy/autophagy regulation in neurons.

papers.title: Estrogen/autophagy/ECSCR regulatory axis in vascular endothelial cells facilitates angiogenesis in endometriosis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how estrogen influences autophagy in vascular endothelial cells, and how this relationship affects the protein ECSCR to promote angiogenesis in endometriosis. The study proposes a regulatory axis connecting hormone signaling, cellular self-degradation processes, and blood vessel formation in this gynecological condition. The findings suggest that targeting autophagy or ECSCR could be a therapeutic strategy for endometriosis-related vascular growth.
papers.why: This paper is only tangentially relevant as it explores autophagy regulation in a non-neuronal, peripheral vascular context unrelated to brain interneurons or perineuronal nets.
